item.title: Individual Differences in Sustained Attention Tune Semantic Abstraction in Neural Encoding of Narratives
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Neural encoding modeling for narrative comprehension -- using LLM embeddings to predict the temporal dynamics of neural activation -- is widely used to evaluate how well the brain represents certain semantic information. This approach, however, typically collapses semantic representation into a scalar fidelity score aggregated across participants, overlooking potentially rich individual differences and qualitative differences in naturalistic neural representations. In the current study, we addressed this gap by investigating how neural semantic encoding varies across individuals with sustained attention, and whether this difference is qualitative in addition to quantitative. Using fMRI data from 49 participants listening to an audiobook, Le Petit Prince, in English, we trained encoding models with GPT-2 embeddings at varying layers and forecasting lengths. Encoding models trained on high-level embeddings (from the 8th layer of GPT-2) showed significant brain-LLM alignment in 73 of 122 cortical and subcortical ROIs, concentrated in the temporal cortex and the default mode network. Functional connectivity strength in a validated connectome-based predictive model of sustained attention correlated with encoding performance in 18 ROIs, most strongly in the insula and in control and attention networks, with no ROI showing significant opposite relationship. Decomposing semantic information by levels of abstraction showed that the neural signature of sustained attention was selectively associated with a greater proportion of high-level gist information encoded in the frontoparietal and attention networks, while the opposite relationship emerged for proportion of low-level information. Sustained attention scores further predicted stronger predictive coding of upcoming narrative content across multiple networks across the whole brain (control, default mode, salience/ventral attention, limbic, and somatomotor networks). These findings suggest that sustained attention does not uniformly amplify neural semantic encoding, but instead shifts neural representations toward more compressed, gist-level formats that support anticipation of upcoming content. Individual differences in brain-LLM alignment can be a signature of representational strategy rather than noise, with potential utility for cognitive phenotyping.

item.title: Neural correlates of infant dialect discrimination: An fNIRS study.
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The present study investigated the neural correlates of infant discrimination of very similar linguistic varieties (Quebecois and Parisian French) using functional Near InfraRed Spectroscopy. In line with previous behavioral and electrophysiological data, there was no evidence that 3-month-olds discriminated the two regional accents, whereas 5-month-olds did, with the locus of discrimination in left anterior perisylvian regions. These neuroimaging results suggest that a developing language network relying crucially on left perisylvian cortices sustains infants’ discrimination of similar linguistic varieties within this early period of infancy.

item.title: Plasticity in Human Brain Language Areas After Stroke: What Can the Right Hemisphere Do?
item.description:
The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
Among the most devastating effects stroke can have on the lives of survivors and those around them are language production and comprehension impairments. The most notable of them - often given the joint diagnostic label of "aphasia" despite their heterogeneity and dissociability - are associated with damage to the brain's left hemisphere, which, in large part for this reason, is considered the "language-dominant" hemisphere. However, the right hemisphere's contribution to language should not be underestimated and may in fact be key to understanding the possibilities and limitations of neuroplasticity for supporting language recovery after stroke. Thus, in this review, we focus on the role of the right hemisphere in supporting human language function, in the neurologically healthy brain and after stroke. We discuss the remarkable capability of the right hemisphere to support normal language abilities after a large left-hemisphere stroke early in life, the more limited capacity for right-hemisphere language support after left-hemisphere stroke in adulthood, and potential interactions between typically left-hemisphere dominant "core" language functions with language functions typically thought to be right-hemisphere dominant, such as emotional prosody. We conclude by highlighting gaps in current knowledge and suggesting areas for future research.

item.title: Beyond Agrammatism: Syntax Processing in Chinese Primary Progressive Aphasia
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Syntax processing impairment is a defining feature of primary progressive aphasia (PPA), particularly in the nonfluent/agrammatic variant. However, current models are derived largely from Indo-European languages, and it remains unclear whether the cognitive and neuroanatomical mechanisms of syntax processing generalize to Chinese, an analytic, pro-drop language that encodes grammatical relationships primarily through word order and function words rather than inflectional morphology. Participants were recruited from the international Chinese Language Assessment in PPA cohort and included 64 individuals with PPA (19 logopenic, 15 nonfluent/agrammatic, 15 semantic, and 15 unclassifiable/mixed) and 60 cognitively healthy controls. Participants completed sentence comprehension and production tasks with systematically manipulated syntactic features. Item-level linguistic determinants were examined using ridge regression, diagnostic performance using receiver operating characteristic analyses, and neuroanatomical correlates using voxel-based morphometry of structural MRI. Performance on sentence comprehension and production was influenced by grammatical and lexical features. Subject-relative clauses, passive constructions, a higher proportion of function words, longer character length, and greater lexical content were associated with poorer performance among participants with PPA. Sentence comprehension was impaired in the logopenic, nonfluent/agrammatic, and semantic variants, even when isolated to the syntactic component of the sentence comprehension task. Similarly, sentence production was impaired across all PPA variants (all P < 0.01 versus controls). No significant differences were observed among PPA variants. Adjusted receiver operating characteristic analyses demonstrated high discrimination between each PPA variant and controls, with areas under the curve ranging from 0.87 to 0.97 for sentence comprehension-syntax and from 0.91 to 0.97 for sentence production. However, pairwise comparisons showed no significant differences in discriminative performance among PPA variants after correction for multiple comparisons. Both sentence comprehension-syntax and sentence production showed associations with semantic and repetition measures in addition to motor speech measures. Voxel-based morphometry showed that higher sentence comprehension-syntax scores were associated with greater grey matter volume in left frontotemporal and cingulate regions, whereas higher sentence production scores were additionally associated with greater gray matter volume in frontostriatal structures, including the caudate, putamen, and thalamus. Syntactic processing impairment in Chinese-speaking individuals with PPA extends beyond the nonfluent/agrammatic variant and is associated with distributed frontotemporal and frontostriatal regions, as well as lexical-semantic and auditory verbal short term memory mechanisms. These findings suggest that the cognitive and neural manifestations of syntactic impairment may be shaped by language-specific typological properties, underscoring the need for linguistically informed approaches to the assessment and interpretation of PPA.

item.title: Combined eye tracking and electroencephalography during referential selection in dyadic interaction.
item.description:
Behavior research methods
Understanding language in real-world interaction requires methods that integrate auditory, visual, and neural signals. We present a proof-of-concept study combining mobile electroencephalography (EEG) and eye tracking to investigate referential selection during dyadic communication. Using a simplified version of the director task, pairs of participants engaged in naturalistic object-movement instructions while EEG and gaze data were recorded and synchronized via LabStreamingLayer, allowing us to calculate overlap-corrected, regression-based event-related potentials (rERPs) time-locked to spoken nouns and to participants' fixations, focusing on the N400/P300 (300-500 ms) and later (500-800 ms) time windows. Our results show that gaze behavior and fixation-related potentials provide crucial information for interpreting language-related ERPs: Targets competing with occluded referents elicited a stronger posterior positivity consistent with greater attentional demands. Fixation timing systematically modulated neural responses. Contrary to predictions, competitors received little visual attention, indicating that participants prioritized task-relevant information. These findings highlight the potential of multimodal data integration for understanding attentional and predictive mechanisms in real-world communication. Importantly, we show that established analytic techniques, such as artifact subspace reconstruction, independent component analysis, and linear deconvolution for ERP calculation, apply to noisy, naturalistic datasets. In addition, we provide a subsampling sensitivity approach to test the stability of the effects across different sample sizes. This study provides a methodological framework linking gaze and neural activity during interactive language processing. All preprocessing and analysis scripts, along with example datasets, are openly available on OSF ( https://osf.io/5ds4z ; a modified and optimized Python implementation is also available on GitHub: https://github.com/XlinCLab/DGAME ).

item.title: EEG Resting-State Beta Band Dynamic Functional Connectivity Reveals State-Dependent Disruption of Language Network Lateralisation in First-Episode Schizophrenia.
item.description:
Neuropsychologia
Language disorganisation is a core feature of schizophrenia with significant functional consequences. However, its neurophysiological substrates remain poorly characterised, particularly in the early stages of the illness. This study investigated whether first-episode schizophrenia (FES) is associated with disruption in the organisation of language-network lateralisation, using both static and dynamic functional connectivity metrics in the EEG beta band. Thirty-one FES patients and 32 age-matched healthy volunteer subjects (HVS) underwent resting-state 64-channel EEG. Source-level connectivity was estimated using the weighted phase lag index with sliding windows, yielding 979 connectivity matrices per participant. Brain network states (BNS) were identified via k-means clustering. Static connectivity was obtained by time-averaging. Temporal features, graph-theoretical metrics, and language-network laterality indices were extracted for both whole-network and language-specific analyses. Group comparisons used permutation-based tests with family-wise error correction. Static connectivity yielded no significant group differences in any metric. Dynamic analysis identified six BNS. FES showed a significant increase in the variability of the temporal dynamics and graph-theory features of BNS5, a state characterised by parieto-occipital dominance. The core language network laterality index was significantly reduced in FES within BNS1, a state characterised by auditory-visual dominance. BNS1 occurrence correlated negatively with language disorganisation scores. Dynamic BNS-specific language network metrics correlated with verbal fluency performance exclusively in FES. These findings demonstrate that language dysfunction in early psychosis is expressed as state-dependent disruption of brain network stability and language lateralisation, detectable only through dynamic connectivity analysis.

item.title: Symptom-related damage patterns in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis.
item.description:
Epilepsia
Objective This study was undertaken to elucidate the neuroanatomical and network substrates underlying diverse seizure symptoms in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis (mTLE-HS) by applying multivariate support vector regression (SVR) to individualized structural symptom mapping and atrophy network mapping (ANM). Methods We retrospectively enrolled 216 patients with mTLE-HS and 460 healthy controls. Six non-mutually exclusive seizure symptoms were assessed. We performed left-right flipping of all images of right-sided mTLE-HS patients along the midline before processing the data. Individual atrophy gray matter maps were derived using normative modeling. Structural symptom mapping was performed using multivariate SVR lesion-symptom mapping. For each patient, indirect ANM maps were generated using a normative functional connectome and direct ANM maps using the patient's own resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Correspondence between the two ANM approaches was assessed using individual-level whole-brain spatial correlations of unthresholded maps and group-level Dice coefficients of thresholded maps. Results Individual structural atrophy patterns were spatially heterogeneous, whereas different seizure manifestations were associated with partially distinct structural patterns and more spatially convergent network-level associations. Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures were associated with thalamic network involvement, gestural/limb automatisms with anterior cingulate-related networks, ictal vocalization symptoms with perisylvian language networks, dysmnesia with hippocampal-posteromedial networks, emotional phenomena with prefrontal-temporal networks, and autonomic phenomena with medial prefrontal and limbic networks. Furthermore, limited spatial correspondence was observed between the results of the direct and indirect atrophy network analyses, suggesting the indirect and direct ANM can be regarded as nonequivalent but potentially complementary approaches. Significance In mTLE-HS, heterogeneous seizure manifestations are associated with distinct patterns of atrophy and distributed functional network involvement. ANM provides a complementary framework for characterizing symptom-related network patterns, and differences between indirect/normative and direct/patient-specific connectome analyses may provide complementary information.

item.title: Modeling Paralinguistic Features for Speech Neuroprostheses: A Systematic Review
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Recent advances in brain-computer interface (BCI) technology have brought speech neuroprostheses closer to restoring naturalistic communication for individuals with severe motor or speech impairments. Although current systems can decode phonemic and lexical information from cortical activity, they often fail to capture paralinguistic dimensions such as intonation, prosody, loudness, and affect that are essential for conveying emotion and intent. This review synthesizes emerging research on modeling and incorporating paralinguistic features into speech neuroprosthetic design. Foundational studies have mapped the cortical organization of speech production, identifying articulatory somatotopy within the sensorimotor cortex and functional subdivisions across planning, phonological, and semantic representations. More recent work has characterized expressive encoding within the ventral precentral and supplementary motor areas, while peripheral and multimodal sensing approaches have demonstrated promising accuracy in decoding emotional states. Collectively, these findings signal a shift toward closed-loop neuroprosthetic systems that integrate affective modulation with linguistic decoding, enabling restoration of speech that is not only intelligible but expressively human.

item.title: 5-Aminolevulinic Acid-Guided Glioma Resection During Awake Craniotomy: Systematic Review of Functional Safety and Oncologic Benefit
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Introduction: Maximal safe resection remains the cornerstone of glioma surgery, particularly in eloquent regions where oncologic gain must be balanced against functional preservation. While 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) fluorescence-guided surgery improves extent of resection in high-grade gliomas under general anesthesia, its role during awake craniotomy (AC) remains underdeveloped. We aimed to evaluate the oncologic and functional outcomes of 5-ALA-guided tumor resection during AC. Methods PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to February 2026 for studies reporting original data on AC using 5‑ALA following PRISMA guidelines. Study quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Results Across 10 studies comprising 108 patients, fluorescence positivity was 76.5% in high‑grade gliomas and 17.5% in low‑grade gliomas. Gross‑total resection was achieved in 57.4% overall, reaching 66.7% in the largest cohort. Transient aphasia occurred in 25.9% of patients, while permanent aphasia and persistent hemiparesis were observed in 8.3% and 14.8%, respectively. In multiple studies, resection was intentionally halted despite persistent fluorescence when functional mapping identified an eloquent cortex, underscoring that mapping remained the decisive determinant of surgical boundaries. No study reported conversion to general anesthesia. Conclusions 5‑ALA-guided resection during AC appears feasible, functionally safe, and clinically useful, particularly for high-grade gliomas in eloquent regions. Across the available literature, 5-ALA consistently enhances intraoperative tumor visualization, supports identification of residual fluorescent disease, and integrates well with cortical and subcortical mapping without clear evidence of increased permanent neurological morbidity. Although functional mapping remains the decisive determinant of the final resection boundary, the available evidence supports 5-ALA as a valuable complementary adjunct in onco-functional glioma surgery. Prospective multicenter studies with standardized volumetric and survival endpoints are now needed to refine patient selection and quantify its added benefit.

item.title: Brain-thought states during movie-watching reflect shared sensory anchors and film- and person- specific processes in association cortex
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Naturalistic paradigms such as movie-watching have transformed functional neuroimaging by capturing cognitive dynamics during rich, real-world experiences. A fundamental challenge, however, is determining whether the neural signatures identified during these experiences reflect general principles of cognition or the specific contexts in which they are measured. To address this question, we combined fMRI data from participants watching eight diverse films with continuous reports of ongoing thought. We found that the generalizability of brain-thought relationships depends on the cognitive process being recruited. Neural signatures linked to sensory processing remained robust across films, whereas those involving memory-related association networks depended on how we modelled between-film variability, indicating that cognition becomes increasingly context-dependent along the cortical hierarchy from sensory to association cortex. Within default and limbic networks, we identified two contrasting memory-related states with opposite consequences for comprehension. One, reflecting the integration of prior knowledge with ongoing experience, predicted better narrative comprehension and was revealed only after accounting for between-film variability. The other, associated with stimulus-independent thought, predicted poorer comprehension and emerged only when between-film variability was not modelled. Together, these findings establish when brain-experience relationships measured during naturalistic paradigms can generalize across contexts and when they instead reflect interactions between cognition and the specific environments in which cognition unfolds. More broadly, the consistency of a given brain-experiential association may depend less on where it occurs in the brain and more on the viewer’s contextual experience: perceiving the film, drawing on memory to understand it, or drifting away. Significance statement Films have revolutionized how we study healthy and atypical brain activity by capturing synchronized, semi-unconstrained dynamics of real-world cognition. Yet experience is rarely measured alongside brain activity, and most studies use one or few films; thus, we do not know whether these neural and experiential responses generalize across films. By combining brain imaging with continuous reports of ongoing thought, we find a hierarchy: sensory processing is consistent across films, whereas memory-related processes in association cortex are uniquely sensitive to how film context is modelled. Two opposing memory states relate to comprehension. One draws on memory to support understanding; the other reflects stimulus-independent thought and impairs it. Identifying brain–experience relationships across films is crucial for developing and understanding naturalistic neuroscience.

item.title: Multimodal modeling of the ictal onset zone in refractory insular epilepsy and seizure outcome of magnetic resonance-guided laser interstitial therapy: A pediatric single-center retrospective study.
item.description:
Epilepsia
Objective This study was undertaken to evaluate seizure outcomes after magnetic resonance-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (MRgLITT) in children with insular epilepsy and to assess how the extent of ablation overlaps with multimodal definitions of the ictal onset zone (IOZ). Methods We conducted a retrospective, single-center study including consecutive pediatric patients treated with MRgLITT for insular epilepsy. All patients underwent presurgical evaluation including electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI); fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) and stereo-EEG (SEEG) were performed in negative-MRI cases. Epileptic zone was identified by visual analysis of SEEG recording. Postablation contrast-enhancing volumes were manually segmented and coregistered with IOZ estimates derived from Multi-centre Epilepsy Lesion Detection (MELD) MRI analysis, FDG-PET voxel-based analysis, and the Epileptogenicity Index, when available. Spatial concordance between modalities was assessed using Dice similarity coefficients, and the proportion of each IOZ modality encompassed within the ablation volume was correlated with postoperative seizure outcomes (International League Against Epilepsy classification). Results Eight children (median age = 10.4 years, range = 2.3-17) were included, with a median postoperative follow-up of 38 months. Two patients had insular tumors, and both achieved seizure freedom after complete ablation. Among the six MRI-negative patients, FDG-PET revealed insular hypometabolism in four, MELD detected a median of one insular cluster (range 1-3), and SEEG identified focal insular ictal activity in three cases. Overall, four negative-MRI patients achieved seizure freedom: three after MRgLITT alone and one after MRgLITT combined with frontal opercular resection. One transient postoperative aphasia was observed. Intermodality spatial concordance was low across all comparisons. A greater proportion of FDG-PET hypometabolism included in the ablation volume was associated with better seizure outcomes (p = .012). Significance MRgLITT is an effective and safe treatment option for focal insular epilepsy in children, either as standalone therapy or in a combined approach. Optimal outcome depends on accurate preoperative delineation of the IOZ and its complete ablation.

item.title: Cerebral Attack With Cortical-Leptomeningeal Involvement and Seizures in AQP4-IgG-Positive Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder.
item.description:
Internal medicine (Tokyo, Japan)
Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) rarely presents with corticalleptomeningeal involvement. A 47-year-old woman with aquaporin-4 immunoglobulin G (AQP4-IgG)-positive NMOSD developed acute headache, seizures, motor aphasia, and worsening right arm weakness. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed a tumefactive-appearing left frontal cortical-subcortical lesion with leptomeningeal enhancement. The clinical and radiological abnormalities improved after immunotherapy. This case illustrates a rare cerebral manifestation of AQP4-IgG-positive NMOSD with cortical-leptomeningeal involvement, seizures, and a tumefactive lesion.

item.title: Functional and Structural Imaging Features of Cognitive Profiles in Multiple Sclerosis.
item.description:
Neurology(R) neuroimmunology & neuroinflammation
Background and objectives Cognitive impairment affects 40%-70% of patients with multiple sclerosis (MS). Although recent hypothesis-driven and data-driven efforts have identified cognitive phenotypes, functional substrates underlying impairment in such phenotypes are still not clear. Our objective was to identify distinct cognitive phenotypes using clustering in a large cohort of patients with MS and characterize their associated clinical, structural MRI, and resting-state (RS) functional connectivity (FC) features. Methods We conducted an observational, cross-sectional study with right-handed patients with MS and age-matched and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs) who underwent neurologic and neuropsychological evaluation (Brief Repeatable Battery of Neuropsychological tests). Latent profile analysis on cognitive test Z-scores identified MS cognitive phenotypes. 3.0T MRI was used to derive atrophy measures and RS FC within default mode network (DMN I/II), executive control network (ECN), left/right fronto-parietal, language, and salience networks. Linear regression models compared structural MRI and RS FC across cognitive phenotypes and HCs, while polynomial contrasts assessed RS FC patterns across groups. Results Three hundred and sixty-nine patients with MS and 168 HCs were enrolled. Four cognitive phenotypes were detected: preserved cognition ([PC], n = 67[18.2%]), mild single-domain verbal fluency involvement (MSD-VF, n = 37[10.0%]), mild single-domain attention involvement (MSD-A, n = 197[53.4%]), and severe multidomain (SMD) involvement (SMD, n = 68[18.4%]). At corrected threshold, PC patients showed decreased deep gray matter (GM) volumes (p < 0.001-0.001) and similar RS FC vs HCs, whereas MSD-VF exhibited no significant atrophy and no differences in RS FC vs HCs. MSD-A displayed lower cortical/deep GM volumes vs HCs (p < 0.001-0.005), whereas SMD had worse clinical and atrophy features (p < 0.001-0.04), as well as decreased DMN II RS FC (p = 0.01-0.04) vs other groups. Polynomial contrast analyses revealed significant quadratic patterns with increased RS FC in MSD-VF vs HC/PC groups, followed by decrease in MSD-A and SMD, within DMN II (p = 0.005), ECN (p = 0.005), and language network (p < 0.001). Discussion PC exhibited intact RS FC, whereas SMD presented widespread structural and DMN RS FC damage. These findings advance our understanding of cognitive heterogeneity in MS by revealing distinct structural and functional neuroimaging profiles across cognitive phenotypes, encouraging future longitudinal and multimodal investigations to improve disease characterization and prognostic stratification.

item.title: Cellular senescence changes and their association with brain structure in schizophrenia and major depressive disorder
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Individuals with schizophrenia (SZ) and major depressive disorder (MDD) may experience accelerated biological aging, potentially linked to cellular senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). While the SASP index has been reported to be elevated in MDD, its status in SZ and its relationship with brain structure remain unclear. This study investigated whether the SASP index, a composite biomarker-based measure, is elevated in SZ and MDD, and examined its associations with brain-predicted age difference (brain-PAD) and regional brain morphology across SZ, MDD, and healthy controls (HCs). A total of 119 subjects (29 individuals with SZ, 40 individuals with MDD, and 50 HCs) underwent both peripheral blood collection and MRI scanning. First, across all subjects, the effects of diagnostic groups on SASP indices were assessed. Second, associations between age-adjusted SASP indices and brain-PAD were examined within each diagnostic group. Third, exploratory analyses tested associations between SASP indices and subcortical volumes as well as cortical thickness and surface area in each diagnostic group. We found a significant main effect of diagnostic group on SASP indices and significantly elevated SASP indices in both SZ and MDD. Although no significant associations were observed between SASP indices and brain-PAD in any diagnostic group, negative associations were identified in SZ between SASP indices and the surface area of the left transverse temporal gyrus and the right inferior frontal gyrus pars triangularis, regions that play pivotal roles in auditory and language processing alterations observed in SZ. These findings suggest that SASP-related processes may contribute to the neural underpinnings of SZ through localized, rather than global, alterations in brain structure.

item.title: Stimulation-stability and preclinical bench testing of a new auditory nerve interface.
item.description:
Bioelectronic medicine
Objective Cochlear implants are the flagship sensory neural prosthetic, enabling improved hearing and speech perception in >1 million patients with hearing loss. Despite over three decades of active work and innovations in cochlear implants, hearing performance for complex tasks such as speech-in-noise and music appreciation are still quite limited, putatively due to the challenge of selectively stimulating the auditory nerve with intracochlear electrodes through the bony cochlear wall. Our approach is to more selectively evoke hearing percepts through the development of an Auditory Nerve Implant (ANI) device that uses penetrating microelectrodes placed directly in the nerve for stimulation, and which will be evaluated through psychophysical testing as part of a first-in-human study. Stability and integrity of ANI electrodes during passive soaking and stimulation are needed to support initiation of the clinical trial, which we evaluated through thermal accelerated saline soak testing and stimulation stability testing. Methods The ANI electrode stability in saline was assessed by accelerated aging at ≥ 67 [Formula: see text]C with a 1.5-year equivalent endpoint using electrode impedance and microscopy to characterize outcomes. Stimulation stability testing evaluated electrode integrity after 6.3 billion pulses at 100 μA, which is the maximum clinical stimulation intensity, for a one-year equivalent use, and 1200 μA, for a high-dose protocol. Electrode impedance, longitudinal stimulation voltage, and microscopy outcomes were used to the quantify results. Results All electrodes had stable impedances around 2 kΩ at the end of the accelerated soak test, except for three with higher impedances but still below the 70 kΩ failure criteria. All but one electrode survived stimulation stability testing. Optical and electron microscopy largely showed little to no change during testing, indicating no observable tip degradation, with the exception of one soak-test device. Conclusions The outcomes from the studies indicate that ANI electrodes exhibit a high degree of integrity and impedance stability. Microscopy characterization proved effective for evaluating electrodes, providing complementary information to standard Backscattered Scanning Electron Microscopy (BSEM). This study suggests the ANI device tolerate a 1.5 year in-dwelling period for a 1 year perceptual study of stimulation evoked percepts, paving the way for clinical translation.

item.title: Osteocalcin and impaired cerebral resting-state functional connectivity in postmenopausal osteoporosis: a pilot case-control study.
item.description:
Postgraduate medicine
Purpose Postmenopausal osteoporosis and circulating osteocalcin have been suggested to influence brain function. Objectives aim to explore associations between brain network resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) connectivity, bone status, and circulating osteocalcin with the hypothesis of an impairment of the bone-brain axis in osteoporosis. Methods This pilot fMRI case-control study included postmenopausal osteoporosis women and matched healthy volunteers, and took place in University Hospital, Clermont-Fd, France. Endpoints were the comparisons between cases and controls of intra- and internetworks connectivity and correlations with bone mineral density (BMD) and osteocalcin. Results Twenty women with osteoporosis and ten matched healthy volunteers were included. Salience, visual and language intranetwork connectivity were all decreased compared to controls (False Discovery Rate (FDR)-corrected p = 0.006, 0.0132 and 0.0199, respectively). Internetwork connectivity was also impaired. For visual network, with three regions of the default mode (p-FDR = 0.0265, 0.0296 and 0.0265) and one with dorsal attention network (p-FDR = 0.0296), and for salience, with dorsal attention networks (p-FDR = 0.0494). Circulating osteocalcin correlated with connectivity between right anterior insula (salience network) and bilateral intraparietal sulci (dorsal attention network) (p-FDR = 0.0145 right side, p-FDR = 0.0421 left side). BMD correlated with connectivity between left regions of the dorsal attention and language networks (p-FDR = 0.0164). Conclusion This pilot study suggests possible impairment of brain connectivity and compensatory protective mechanisms/maladaptive mechanisms in postmenopausal osteoporosis. It also unveils that lower osteocalcin concentrations and BMD may be associated with altered cerebral connectivity, confirming animal studies, and providing preliminary findings for further research.

item.title: The role of world knowledge in sentence comprehension under working-memory constraints: An fMRI study
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Introduction Comprehension of thematic roles, i.e., “who did what to whom,” relies on limited cognitive resources, and constraints on these resources can alter the use of plausibility information derived from world knowledge. Although sentence-processing studies have described how plausibility information constrains interpretation, it remains unclear how this process is supported by the architecture of working memory. This study examines whether the phonological loop, one of the components of working memory, contributes to thematic-role processing based on world knowledge. Methods Using articulatory suppression and functional magnetic resonance imaging, we examined whether constraining the function of the phonological loop modulates behavioral and neural responses to sentences in which syntactically assigned thematic roles are plausible or implausible given world knowledge. To constrain the phonological loop, we manipulated the task: a single task and a dual task involving concurrent articulation. Results We found no significant interaction between task and plausibility, although equivalence analyses did not provide evidence for the absence of a plausibility effect during articulation. In contrast, a robust main effect of thematic-role plausibility was observed: implausible sentences elicited greater activation than plausible sentences in the left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG) and medial superior frontal gyrus (mSFG) at the whole-brain level, and in both the pars triangularis and pars orbitalis of the LIFG in the ROI analyses. Discussion These findings provide no conclusive evidence that constraining the phonological loop substantially modulates the use of world knowledge in comprehension of thematic roles, while also leaving open the possibility of a smaller task-dependent effect. At the same time, the robust neural responses to implausibility indicate that the LIFG and mSFG consistently contribute to the processing of plausibility information derived from world knowledge.

item.title: Openness to Experience Modulates the Neural Dynamics of Semantic Processing.
item.description:
Physiology & behavior
Personality fundamentally shapes language processing, yet the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. Openness to Experience (openness), as measured by the NEO Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI), has been associated with enhanced creativity and engagement with novel semantic information. This study examined how openness modulates neural dynamics of semantic processing using event-related potentials (ERPs) during a semantic category verification task. Participants evaluated category relatedness across four levels of semantic structure, including high typicality (HT), low typicality (LT), related violations (RV), and nonrelated violations (NRV). Neural responses exhibited the expected graded pattern, with N400 amplitudes increasing as semantic relatedness decreased. Critically, higher Openness was associated with greater N400 differentiation between related and nonrelated violations, an effect uniquely predicted by Openness beyond the remaining four personality traits. Follow-up analyses revealed that this differentiation was primarily driven by enhanced N400 responses to nonrelated violations rather than by reduced responses to related violations. This pattern is inconsistent with a simple facilitation account in which higher Openness uniformly eases semantic processing. Instead, it suggests that Openness is associated with heightened sensitivity to semantic mismatch or more sustained semantic evaluation when incoming information is incompatible with an activated context. Behavioral performance was comparable across participants; the observed neural differences were not accompanied by detectable differences in task success. Together, these findings establish that Openness is systematically related to variation in the neural dynamics of semantic processing, while highlighting the need to clarify the underlying cognitive mechanisms and contributions of other individual differences.

item.title: Neurophysiological signatures underlying preserved lexical-semantic proficiency in healthy aging.
item.description:
Neurobiology of aging
Although semantic cognition remains behaviorally stable with age, neuroimaging studies report age-related alterations in response to semantic context. To address these inconsistent findings, we combined behavioral and magnetoencephalography (MEG) measures and examined the neural mechanisms underlying lexical-semantic processing in healthy aging. Forty-six Finnish-speaking adults across younger (22 - 32 years) and older (62 - 69 years) cohorts performed a semantic congruency judgment task on word pairs. Both age groups performed the task with high accuracy, with older adults responding faster than younger. While task performance was retained in older adults, MEG revealed a shift in the neural activation patterns with advancing age. Younger participants exhibited the canonical N400 effect in the left temporal cortex 300 - 400 ms post-stimulus, followed by a late semantic effect, whereas older adults showed less pronounced congruency effects, and the activation distribution was shifted toward frontal and bilateral regions. Despite the absence of the canonical N400 effect in older participants, multivariate time-resolved decoding demonstrated that the congruency effect was decodable from the MEG activation patterns in both groups from ~300 ms post-stimulus, indicating preserved sensitivity to congruency with age. Decoding performance further correlated with response times, suggesting that greater neural separation between semantic concepts, indicated by higher decodability, is associated with rapid decision-making. Critically, age groups were distinguishable based on their neural responses 300 - 800 ms post-stimulus, indicating a functional reorganization of semantic processing in older adults. Overall, our findings suggest that healthy aging involves a reconfiguration of neural systems associated with preserved semantic proficiency, despite broader age-related cognitive changes.

item.title: Altered frontal and dorsal hemodynamic engagement during mandarin aspiration processing in post-stroke aphasia: an fNIRS study.
item.description:
Brain and language
Auditory and speech-perception difficulties are common in post-stroke aphasia (PSA), but cortical responses during passive listening to Mandarin speech remain underexplored. Seventeen Mandarin-speaking individuals with PSA and 18 matched healthy controls listened to auditory oddball blocks containing /ba/ standards and /pa/ deviants during functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Although these syllables instantiate an aspiration contrast strongly cued by voice onset time (VOT), standard and deviant trials were combined within a single block-level condition. The resulting measures therefore indexed activation during speech-containing blocks relative to silent inter-block intervals rather than phonemic discrimination, categorization, or VOT-specific processing. Seven theory-driven channels covering bilateral auditory, sensorimotor, inferior frontal, and dorsolateral prefrontal regions were analyzed using three HbO indices: β coefficient, peak amplitude, and temporal centroid. The PSA group showed an overall reduction in task-related HbO activation, reflected by a significant Group effect for the β coefficient. Peak amplitude also showed significant Group and Group × Channel effects, although no individual channel remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Temporal centroid showed no significant group or interaction effects. These findings provide preliminary evidence for reduced block-evoked cortical recruitment during passive auditory exposure to Mandarin speech sounds in PSA. Because the analysis did not include a direct standard-deviant or active auditory control comparison, the findings do not establish a selective impairment of phonemic discrimination, categorization, or VOT processing. Because patients were assessed 6-7 months after stroke onset, the activation differences may reflect both persistent impairment and recovery-related reorganization during the early chronic stage.

item.title: Predictors of Insufficient Awakening During Awake Surgery: A Single-Center Retrospective Study.
item.description:
Operative neurosurgery (Hagerstown, Md.)
Background and objectives Awake surgery (AS) is widely performed for the resection of brain tumors and for epilepsy surgery. However, a non-negligible proportion of patients experience insufficient intraoperative awakening, leading to inadequate neurological monitoring. This retrospective study investigated predictive factors associated with insufficient intraoperative awakening. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 78 consecutive AS procedures for brain tumors and epilepsy performed at our institution between 2021 and 2024. Previously reported predictive factors for AS failure and contraindications for AS were evaluated, along with the presence of basal ganglionic involvement (BGI), defined as a high-intensity area on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery imaging involving the striatum and globus pallidus. Results Insufficient intraoperative awakening occurred in 13 cases (16.7%). Age (odds ratio [OR] per year, 1.04; 95% CI, 1.00-1.08), aphasia (OR, 4.18; 95% CI, 1.23-15.5), midline shift (OR, 7.85; 95% CI, 2.22-30.6), and BGI (OR, 118; 95% CI, 18.7-2352.2) were identified as factors associated with insufficient awakening using univariate logistic regression analysis. In multivariate logistic regression analysis, BGI remained independently associated with insufficient awakening (OR, 104.7; 95% CI, 16.4-2098.1). Preoperative corticosteroids were administered to 11 patients with glioblastoma to reduce peritumoral edema. Among 7 patients with glioblastoma and BGI at admission, BGI resolved preoperatively in 2 patients after corticosteroid therapy, and AS was successfully performed in both cases. Betamethasone was predominantly used, at a median dose of 4 mg/day and median preoperative treatment duration of 14 days. In both cases with resolved BGI, betamethasone was administered at 8 mg/day for more than 10 days. Conclusion BGI may be one of the independent predictors of insufficient intraoperative awakening across a broader AS population. Preoperative administration of an adequate course of betamethasone may facilitate sufficient intraoperative awakening in patients with glioblastoma and BGI. Further multicenter studies are warranted.

item.title: Striatal network dysfunction underlying speech impairment in early Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
NPJ Parkinson's disease
The pathophysiology underlying Parkinson's disease (PD) speech impairments and its potential sex differences remain unclear. We investigated sex-specific alterations in speech and striato-cortical networks in 104 patients with early PD (68M/36F), and 44 healthy controls (23M/21F), using quantitative speech markers and multimodal neuroimaging. Speech features related to prosody, phonation, articulation, fluency, and rhythm, were extracted from voice recordings; striatal dopaminergic loss was quantified using DaT-SPECT, and functional connectivity between striatal and cortical language networks was analyzed with resting-state fMRI. Results showed that PD-related speech impairments were more pronounced in males. Functional connectivity was globally reduced in PD, but female patients exhibited higher caudate-cortical connectivity. In males, speech deficits were associated with both dopaminergic loss and connectivity disruption, whereas in females, only connectivity changes were involved. These findings revealed sex-specific pathophysiological mechanisms in early PD speech disorders, emphasizing the need for sex-stratified approaches in research and clinical practice.

item.title: From Contrasts to Representations: Rethinking fMRI Approaches for Cortico-Cerebellar Networks.
item.description:
Cerebellum (London, England)
The relationship between the cerebellum and cerebrum remains poorly understood in the neuroimaging literature, despite decades of functional magnetic resonance (fMRI) research. In this opinion article, we argue that this gap reflects fundamental methodological constraints rather than merely a lack of scientific interest. We first discuss challenges in acquiring fMRI data and analysis, with an emphasis on the cerebellum. We then critically evaluate the most common analysis approaches including functional connectivity, univariate contrasts, multivariate pattern analysis, and encoding models, examining the contributions and limitations of each to identify and quantify cortico-cerebellar networks. Through the lens of language processing, we briefly review how these approaches have been applied to characterize cortico-cerebellar networks underlying cognitive function. We conclude by proposing that encoding model frameworks, combined with ecologically valid naturalistic paradigms, offer advantages that can help resolve longstanding debates about cortico-cerebellar network function and organization.

item.title: Modulation of the speed of Intrinsic Alpha Frequency (IAF) with tACS modulates variability of illusory speech perception
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Navigating the world requires our brains to constantly process a massive influx of information from the environment. One of the most remarkable yet complex feats the human brain performs daily is speech perception. It is a multifaceted, hierarchical process that relies heavily on the integration of auditory and visual cues, particularly in noisy environments. Neural integration of these streams is hypothesized to depend on temporal mechanisms governed by individual alpha frequency (IAF, 8-12 Hz), which serves as a key neural correlate of the temporal binding window (TBW). While IAF has been linked to multisensory integration, its role in shaping multisensory illusions remains largely unexplored. Here, we tested this directly using transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to modulate occipital activity during multisensory conflict. In a two-day protocol involving 27 healthy participants, resting-state EEG was recorded to determine IAF. On Day 2, participants then performed a multisensory speech task involving congruent (pa/, /ta/, /ka/) and incongruent McGurk stimuli (auditory /pa/, visual /ka/), both at baseline and during tACS applied at IAF and offset frequencies (IAF ± 2 Hz) over occipital electrodes. While accuracy for congruent syllables remained high across conditions, results revealed that tACS significantly reduced the perception of illusory /ta/ percepts during McGurk trials. Finally, using a phenomenological model based on Kuramoto oscillators, we provided a mechanistic explanation for the percentage of illusory responses observed across participants under the influence of tACS at IAF and offsets. This study highlights the potential for targeted neuromodulatory interventions to influence multisensory processing in clinical or professional settings.

item.title: Spoken language comprehension relies on context-dependent neural weighting of syntax and prosody
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Comprehending spoken language requires extracting syntactic structure and meaning from a continuous acoustic signal. Psycholinguistic evidence points to a key role for prosody in this process. However, because interactions between prosody and syntax are typically demonstrated using carefully controlled sentence constructions, it remains unclear whether such interactions constitute a general, default property of spoken language processing. Addressing this question requires naturalistic, broad-coverage data. Here, we combined experimental psycholinguistics with naturalistic neuroscience to investigate the joint neural encoding of syntax and prosody in MEG recordings of 26 participants (19 female) listening to narrative speech. Linguistic annotations revealed that strong prosodic boundaries tend to coincide with syntactic phrase closures, and that the strength of prosodic boundaries scales with the number of phrases closed. Using time-resolved regression with temporal response functions, we modeled how these features relate to delta-band neural activity during continuous speech processing. Our results reveal a bidirectional interaction between syntax and prosody. Prosodic marking modulates the neural processing of syntax, with phrase closures being encoded more strongly when accompanied by strong prosodic boundaries. Conversely, syntactic structure shapes prosodic encoding, such that boundary strength is neurally encoded primarily at points of syntactic phrase closure. These findings demonstrate that syntax and prosody are encoded not independently, but in a context-dependent and mutually constraining manner, highlighting their joint role in guiding structure building during naturalistic spoken language comprehension. Significance statement How the brain transforms continuous sensory stimulation into structured representations is a central question in cognitive neuroscience. Spoken language comprehension provides a particularly compelling case: as the acoustic signal alone underdetermines linguistic meaning, the brain must integrate bottom-up sensory information with top-down linguistic knowledge, such as syntax. Here, we recorded brain activity during audiobook listening to examine how syntax and prosody jointly shape neural responses to narrative speech. We find evidence for a bidirectional neural interaction: prosody modulates the neural encoding of syntax, and syntactic context shapes the neural encoding of prosody. These findings suggest that the brain flexibly integrates bottom-up and top-down information depending on how informative each cue is for extracting structured meaning from naturalistic speech.

item.title: Data-Driven Prediction of Speech-in-Noise Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Machine Learning Models.
item.description:
Annals of biomedical engineering
Purpose Difficulty understanding speech in noise (SIN) is a major determinant of communication ability and quality of life, affecting individuals with hearing loss as well as some with normal hearing. Data-driven prediction methods offer a promising approach for modeling complex, multidimensional factors underlying speech perception. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated computational approaches for predicting SIN-related outcomes, compared predictive performance across model classes where quantitative synthesis was feasible, and identified methodological factors relevant to model selection, generalizability, and clinical translation. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies using machine learning (ML), neural networks, automatic speech recognition (ASR), or auditory model-based approaches to predict, simulate, or evaluate SIN-related outcomes. Quantitative synthesis was performed using random-effects models for studies reporting support vector machine (SVM) or random forest (RF) performance, and between-study heterogeneity was assessed. Results Eligible studies included traditional ML, neural network, ASR-based, and mechanistic auditory modeling approaches. SVM accuracy pooled at 0.71 and SVM area under the curve at 0.84, while RF accuracy pooled at 0.86 and RF recall at 0.81. Bootstrap estimates were broadly consistent with the primary random-effects estimates, although between-study heterogeneity ranged from moderate to very high across analyses. Conclusion Data-driven prediction approaches show promise for predicting SIN-related outcomes, but high heterogeneity precludes identifying a single optimal model. Model selection should reflect the prediction target, data type, sample size, interpretability, and intended use. Current evidence supports proof-of-concept performance more strongly than clinical utility, highlighting the need for larger, standardized, externally validated studies.

item.title: How auditory rhythm perception shapes speech production: The influence of neural synchronization and rhythmic patterns.
item.description:
Psychonomic bulletin & review
Auditory rhythm perception facilitates language processing, yet it remains unclear how neural synchronization to external rhythms contributes to speech production. The present study examined whether individual differences in neural synchronization modulate rhythmic priming effects during speech production and whether such effects depend on the rhythmic structure of the target utterance. Eighty-six native Mandarin speakers performed a speech production task involving two four-syllable rhythmic patterns as targets: the dominant [2+2] pattern (boundary after the second syllable) and the less common [1+3] pattern (boundary after the first syllable). Each target was preceded by a rhythmically congruent or incongruent pure-tone prime. Neural synchronization to the primes was quantified using cerebral-acoustic coherence (CACoh) between EEG activity and the temporal envelope of the auditory rhythms, and rhythmic priming was assessed using response latencies. K-means clustering of CACoh measures identified two participant groups characterized by relatively high and low levels of neural synchronization. Behavioral analyses revealed a significant Group × Target Type interaction. For the less common [1+3] pattern, low synchronizers exhibited reliable rhythmic priming, whereas high synchronizers showed little or no priming benefit. In contrast, priming effects for the dominant [2+2] pattern were modest and comparable across groups. Furthermore, higher theta-band CACoh was associated with smaller priming effects for [1+3] targets, indicating that stronger neural synchronization predicted reduced behavioral facilitation. These findings suggest that the influence of auditory rhythm on speech production depends jointly on individual neural synchronization capacity and the rhythmic structure of the planned utterance. The results provide new evidence that auditory-motor interactions in speech production are shaped by both listener-specific and utterance-specific factors.

item.title: Increasing cerebellar beta rhythms shifts cerebral oscillatory signatures of context-driven language processing
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
While there is growing consensus that the cerebellum is part of the cerebrally centred network underlying language processing, the direct nature of its contribution to comprehension and production remains unknown. In particular, while both processes require lexical access, production additionally involves motor processes linked to articulatory planning, which has fuelled the view that the cerebellum is primarily involved in motor control in language production. Cortically, both lexical access and articulatory planning are known to be driven by alpha-beta power decreases. To disentangle cerebellar involvement in language, this study investigated the modulatory effect of transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) over the right cerebellum on context-driven language comprehension and production. In a cross-over, double-blind, sham-controlled within-participants design, 32 healthy volunteers received 20 minutes of 20-Hz tACS (2 mA peak-to-peak) targeting the right posterior cerebellum. Immediately afterwards, they performed a context-driven language task while EEG was recorded from 32 channels. In the task, visually presented lead-in sentences creating a constraining or unconstraining context were followed by a picture depicting the final word of the sentence. Participants were instructed to name the picture (production) or judge its animacy (comprehension). Responses became slower overall following active compared to sham tACS, and this increase was more pronounced in the comprehension task. In line with previous work, reliable context-related oscillatory power decreases were observed in response to the context manipulation, but exhibited a different pattern across tasks and stimulation conditions. For production, beta-centred power decreases following sham shifted to temporally and spatially extended alpha power decreases following active tACS. By contrast, alpha-centred power decreases following sham tACS in the comprehension task increased following active tACS. Increasing beta activity in the right posterior cerebellum thus affected early stages of context-driven language processing linked to lexical access in both language domains. The stimulation-induced spectral, spatial and temporal shifts suggest recruitment of alternative cortical resources as a consequence of cerebellar network modulation. This interpretation is consistent with the cerebellum functioning as a network node coordinating temporal dynamics across distributed language regions.

item.title: Neural Correlates of Beat Processing in Infancy and Their Association With Later Grammar Development: Evidence for the Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Infants show evidence of beat processing from birth, but its neural correlates in infancy remain poorly understood. Moreover, although rhythm and grammar abilities are closely linked in older (school-aged) children, it is not known whether individual differences in infant beat processing lay the foundations for those associations. This longitudinal EEG study examined neural correlates of beat processing in 6–12-month-old infants (N=37) and their relation to sentence comprehension skills in the same children at 4 years. We analyzed infants’ evoked time–frequency responses to rhythmic tone–tone–rest sequences presented in physically accented conditions and in inferred-beat conditions, in which accents were removed after an initial exposure phase.. Analyses revealed a significant increase in power to physically accented beats (9–24 Hz, p < .001). Individual differences in this response were positively associated with receptive grammar performance at age 4, assessed with the TROG-2 (r = .48, p = .005), and remained significant after controlling for infant age, parent education, and home music environment (β = .45, p = .011). The inferred beat effect was not related to later sentence comprehension performance. These findings indicate that infant neural activity tracks beat structure, with neural correlates broadly similar to those reported in adults, and that early neural sensitivity to beat is associated with later grammar development, supporting the Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis.

item.title: Testing different metrics for syntactic and morphological complexity in aphasic discourse: A cross-genre comparison in Spanish.
item.description:
Neuropsychologia
Purpose The aim of this study is to determine which of four tasks testing different discourse genres (descriptive, procedural, conversational, and narrative) is the most sensitive in detecting syntactic and morphological complexity deficits in Spanish aphasia. Additionally, we compare two approaches for measuring syntax in discourse to identify the most accurate set of metrics for discriminating group membership. Method In this comparative cross-sectional study, we analyzed the discourse of an aphasia group (N = 20) and a non-brain-damaged group (N = 14). Data was preprocessed using manual and automated procedures. We measured syntactic complexity through proxies (mean length of utterance, noun-verb ratio, and verbs per utterance), in addition to a competing 'syntactic structures' metric. The latter includes variables of subordination, left branching, relative clauses, and word integration, while morphological complexity was measured through an inflectional index. Results The descriptive and narrative tasks highlighted the most significant differences across syntactic complexity metrics between the groups. Additionally, nested binomial logistic regression models showed that the 'syntactic structures' metric predicted groups better than the proxies alone. Conclusions A comprehensive assessment of syntactic complexity can be obtained through the administration of both descriptive and narrative tasks. The measurement of 'syntactic structures' in discourse proved a fitter and finer-grained approach for group discrimination than the incorporation of syntactic proxies alone. These findings provide guidance for a precise discourse assessment in Spanish aphasia.

item.title: Affective prosody and facial expression cues differentially augment spoken sentence and discourse comprehension for acute left and right hemisphere stroke survivors.
item.description:
Neuropsychologia
Comprehension for spoken sentences and discourse is differentially impacted by left- (LH) and right-hemisphere (RH) brain damage, such as that caused by stroke. Comprehension deficits can have disabling effects on one's ability to process information, participate in everyday life, and create and maintain relationships. This cross-sectional, observational study evaluated differences in sentence- and discourse-level comprehension between LH and RH stroke survivors across different prosodic conditions and examined relationships between comprehension and damage to key LH and RH regions. Participants included 43 LH and 46 RH acute stroke survivors and 39 controls. All participants completed an in-house clinical assessment that included short passages presented in three conditions: neutral prosody, affective prosody, and affective prosody plus facial expression cues. Stroke survivors also completed magnetic resonance imaging. Consistent with expectations, stroke participants achieved lower comprehension accuracy than controls across conditions. LH participants' accuracy in the 'affective prosody plus facial expressions' condition was greater than in the neutral prosody condition, and total LH lesion volume was associated with performance. RH participants' accuracy in the 'affective prosody' and 'affective prosody plus facial expressions' conditions was greater than in the neutral prosody condition. Overall, both groups' scores increased linearly from Condition 1 to 3. None of the prespecified LH or RH brain regions were significantly associated with performance. Findings suggest that some acute LH and RH stroke survivors with comprehension deficits can benefit from affective prosody and facial expression cues, but different or additional cues may be needed for greatest benefit.

item.title: Adolescent pragmatic development mirrors pragmatic individual differences in adulthood: An fMRI study.
item.description:
Neuropsychologia
Pragmatic development is still ongoing during adolescence. However, the developmental trajectory during this period is understudied and the underlying neural correlates of pragmatic development are unknown. In this study, we used an established fMRI paradigm contrasting indirect and direct speech acts in a newly acquired adolescent sample (n = 51) and a previously collected adult sample (n = 57). The adolescent sample was subdivided into Young (ages 13-15) and Mid (ages 16-18) groups and the adult sample (Old, ages 20-36) was split based on pragmatic skill level (established in separate behavioral tests). We observed age-related increases in activity in the posterior medial superior frontal gyrus, and a combination of age-related differences and adult individual differences in the dorsal aspects of the posterior cingulate cortex (dPCC). Both clusters were located outside the classic perisylvian language network. We interpret the dPCC findings in terms of its overlap with the Default Mode Network. Similar activity in the dPCC between adolescents and adults with lower pragmatic skill is consistent with a view that a delayed adolescent development may lead to persistent pragmatic difficulties in adulthood. The findings also indicate development towards context-specific processing. By studying adolescence, a presumably uniquely human extended developmental period, we provide a rare empirical angle on the question of which aspects of brain and cultural evolution contributed to the human communicative faculty.

item.title: Dissociable pupil-linked arousal during overt and inner speech.
item.description:
iScience
Inner (covert) speech, the silent production of language in one's mind, plays a central role in human cognition and engages speech-related cortical networks partly overlapping with those for overt speech. Because cortical language processing unfolds within arousal states set by the ascending systems, we asked whether inner and overt speech are accompanied by similar pupil-linked arousal patterns. Using pupillometry across three counting-task experiments, we found a dissociation between inner and overt speech. While overt speech consistently elicited pupil dilation across conditions, inner speech produced a variable dilation profile relative to baseline: pupil constriction (simple counting), no deviation (noun-phrase counting), and clear dilation (step counting; high cognitive load). Importantly, pupil size during inner speech remained smaller than that during overt speech despite task-dependent dynamics. These findings suggest that task-elicited inner speech is accompanied by lower pupil-linked arousal than overt speech, adding a state-level physiological dimension to cortical accounts of verbal processing.

item.title: Scalp acupuncture coupled with speech-language therapy modulates the ventral-dorsal structural brain network in patients with post-stroke anomia: a randomized clinical and DTI neuroimaging trial.
item.description:
Chinese medicine
Background Scalp acupuncture (SA) is used as adjunctive rehabilitation for post-stroke aphasia, but its effect on naming recovery and structural language-network changes remains unclear. We evaluated SA coupled with speech-language therapy (SLT) in patients with post-stroke anomia and explored diffusion tensor imaging markers of ventral-dorsal structural language networks. Methods This randomized controlled trial recruited 85 patients with post-stroke anomia and randomly assigned them to SA or control. Both groups received conventional stroke treatment and SLT; the SA group additionally received scalp acupuncture synchronously with SLT during needle retention. Treatment was delivered once daily, 5 days/week for 4 weeks. The primary outcome was WAB naming total score. Diffusion tensor imaging assessed white matter integrity and topological properties before and after treatment. Results Compared to the control group, the SA group showed greater improvements in the WAB naming total score (P = 0.009), object naming, sentence completion, responsive speech, BNT spontaneous naming, and SAQOL-39 communication. In the ventral-dorsal structural network, the SA group showed smaller changes in the area under the curve (AUC) of small-worldness properties (P = 0.008) and normalized clustering coefficient (P = 0.017), and greater changes in clustering coefficient and local efficiency. In the SA group, the change in small-worldness was negatively correlated with the change in the WAB naming total score (r = -0.451, P = 0.027). The SA group also showed smaller axial diffusivity (AD) changes in the left uncinate fasciculus (P = 0.003, Bonferroni corrected), which correlated negatively with the WAB naming total score change (r = -0.440, P = 0.031). Exploratory adjusted regression showed that SA-group assignment was associated with greater naming improvement after adjustment for baseline naming and clinical covariates. Conclusions SA coupled with SLT was associated with greater naming recovery in patients with post-stroke anomia. The benefit was accompanied by changes in structural language-network topology and white matter integrity, particularly involving the left UF. These findings support further evaluation of scalp acupuncture as an adjunct to language rehabilitation and suggest structural network plasticity as a relevant imaging correlate.

item.title: Auditory- and Visual-Speech Evoked Activation of the Superior Temporal Gyrus Contralateral to the Cochlear Implant Predicts Speech Recognition Outcomes.
item.description:
Ear and hearing
Objectives Speech recognition outcomes vary widely in cochlear implant recipients, but the reasons for this variability are not well explained by patient history factors alone. Neuroplastic reorganization after both deafness and cochlear implant switch-on can affect how new recipients adapt to electrical hearing. In this study, we evaluate the associations between speech recognition outcomes and stimulus-evoked activation of cortical language processing areas. Design Forty-three newly implanted post-lingually deaf adult cochlear implant recipients (17 female, mean age at implantation: 58.5 yr, SD: 14.4 yr) were recruited for the longitudinal study. Participants attended two research visits: the first conducted within 1 mo of device switch-on, and the second conducted 1 yr after device switch-on. At each visit, we evaluated speech recognition outcomes in noise and cortical activation using functional near-infrared spectroscopy during a passive listening task, during which a story was told in either an auditory- or visual-speech (lipreading) condition. Results We found consistent negative correlations between speech understanding outcomes at 1 yr and activation of the superior temporal gyrus at 1 mo in response to both auditory and visual speech. These associations were not observed for activation measured at 1 yr. Subgroup regression analysis revealed that these correlations were most consistently seen in the superior temporal gyrus contralateral to the cochlear implant. Activation in the superior temporal gyrus contralateral to the implant at 1 mo also explained additional variance in speech outcomes at 1 yr beyond clinical factors alone. However, longitudinal analysis showed no association between within-subject changes in activation and changes in speech understanding outcomes within this first year of implant use. Conclusions Our evidence highlights that neuroplastic changes which occur following adult-onset deafness play an important role in how cochlear implant recipients adapt to their devices after switch-on. The relationship between neuroimaging measures made within 1 mo after device switch-on and speech recognition outcomes at 1 yr can potentially enable triaging of recipients to improve clinical management of implant recipients.

item.title: Multidimensional semantic activation in children's discourse reading is associated with their reading ability.
item.description:
Cortex; a journal devoted to the study of the nervous system and behavior
Around fourth grade, children transition from learning-to-read to reading-to-learn, yet how their multidimensional semantic representation during discourse reading differs from that of adults and relates to reading ability remains unclear. This study investigated multidimensional semantic activation in 42 fourth-to sixth-grade children (mean age 10.3 years) and 44 adults (mean age 25.1 years) during story reading using fMRI. Children were stratified by reading ability using inverse efficiency scores from comprehension questions. Semantic activation across six dimensions (visual, motor, social, emotional, spatial, temporal) was modeled using the Six Semantic Dimension Database. Results showed that high-reading-ability children exhibited significantly stronger temporal but weaker social semantic activation compared to adults, whereas low-reading-ability children showed adult-like patterns. Brain-behavior association analyses revealed that multidimensional semantic activation patterns were linked to reading performance in children (explaining 25.0% of variance), whereas no such relationship was evident in adults. Additionally, high-reading-ability children demonstrated enhanced activation in cognitive control networks relative to both low-ability peers and adults. These findings suggest that high-reading-ability children may strategically modulate multidimensional semantic processing through cognitive control to compensate for limited reading experience, highlighting the flexible, strategy-dependent nature of multidimensional semantic representation during developmental reading.

item.title: Extended high frequency hearing influences cortical response amplitudes to speech.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Since young adults hear sounds up to 20 kHz, the loss of extended high-frequency hearing (EHF; above 8 kHz) is a hallmark of age-related hearing loss, often progressing from early lifetime. However, this deficit frequently goes undetected because routine clinical hearing tests and most hearing aids are currently mostly limited to 8 kHz. EHF hearing has been linked to deficits in speech perception in noise and to self-reported hearing. However, it remains elusive how EHF hearing influences speech intelligibility. Here we recorded neuromagnetic brain responses using magnetoencephalography (MEG) within a frequency-tagging speech paradigm designed to probe hierarchical levels of attention and memory-dependent speech processing and recognition. Auditory evoked field (AEF) responses were significantly reduced in both left and right brain hemispheres in individuals with impaired EHF hearing compared to those subjects with better EHF hearing. A gradual reinforcement of left-hemispheric AEF seen over age was not observed in young adults (19-29 y) with preserved EHF hearing. This was linked to stronger auditory brainstem responses (ABR), reflecting better neural synchronized auditory responses at stimulus onset. The reinforced left-hemispheric dominance in young adults with impaired EHF hearing, in contrast, was linked to lower ABRs. Our findings suggest that through its impact on stimulus-onset synchrony to phase locking of oscillations in the auditory cortex, sound energy above 8 kHz contributes to the intelligibility of speech. Together, the results highlight the need to reconsider EHF hearing in both audiological assessment and hearing-aid design.

item.title: Communication as a Two-Person Neural Process: fNIRS Hyperscanning in Adults with and without Post-Stroke Aphasia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Communication is inherently interactive, yet most neuroimaging studies examine individuals in isolation. Here, we used functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning to investigate interbrain synchrony (IBS) during naturalistic communication. In Study 1, 13 healthy familiar dyads completed Joint Singing, Joint Reading, and Picture Guessing tasks. IBS was quantified using wavelet transform coherence across bilateral frontal and temporoparietal regions. Joint Singing produced higher IBS than the other tasks in several regions, including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and temporoparietal junction, and selected effects were greater in true than pseudo-dyads. In Study 2, we applied the same paradigm to five individuals with chronic post-stroke aphasia interacting with trained speech-language pathologists. IBS could be estimated in all dyads after lesion-informed channel exclusion, although regional coverage varied with lesion location. These findings demonstrate that fNIRS hyperscanning can capture task-dependent interpersonal neural coupling during spoken interaction and can be extended to communication involving individuals with aphasia. This approach provides a foundation for studying how neural coordination between communication partners relates to functional communication and partner-supported interaction.

item.title: Functional near infrared spectroscopy-based dual-stream adaptive language mapping in adults with and without post-stroke aphasia
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
In aphasia, variability in lesion location and post-stroke network reorganization complicates efforts to identify the regions that support semantic versus phonological processing. In prior work, researchers have often examined these domains in separate patient cohorts, further limiting direct comparison of their neural substrates within aphasia. To address this gap, we investigated the degree of overlap and specialization within semantic and phonological networks in adults with and without aphasia and examined how neural activity relates to task performance and lesion profiles. Sixteen neurologically healthy adults and 15 participants with aphasia following left hemisphere stroke completed adaptive Semantic Matching and Rhyme Judgment tasks during functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) recording. Changes in oxyhemoglobin and deoxyhemoglobin were measured within regions of interest, and activation was related to standardized task performance and damage to left ventral and dorsal language pathways in participants with aphasia.
